name: Castle Garden Bazaar
description: A neo-Renaissance complex of arcades, stairways and gardens by Miklós Ybl at the foot of Castle Hill, beside the Danube. Built in the 1870s and 1880s, it later served as a rock-concert venue, then as a ruin, before its restoration and reopening in 2014.

children.text: The Castle Garden Bazaar, Várkert Bazár in Hungarian, is a neo-Renaissance complex of arcades, staircases and gardens on the Danube side of Castle Hill, at Ybl Miklós tér. It was built between 1875 and 1883 to plans by Miklós Ybl. According to the building's own history page, the idea arose in the early 1870s of a representative building complex and ornamental garden at the foot of the hill. Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as a listed monument and part of the Budapest World Heritage site.

A history of Buda Castle describes Ybl's design as an open arcade with pavilions, stairways, ramps and two blocks of flats. The arcades were meant to hold shops, stores and workshops, and the neo-Renaissance gardens were laid out to keep an open view of the Danube from the Royal Palace above. The sculptor Alajos Stróbl got the first studio in the arcade, in 1884, and about eighty other artists followed over the next century.

In the second half of the twentieth century the bazaar found a different life as the Budai Ifjúsági Park, the Buda Youth Park, which hosted pop and rock concerts from 1961 to 1984. Visit Hungary names bands such as LGT, Edda, Piramis, P. Mobil, Omega and Beatrice, and says inscriptions by Edda and LGT on a stone wall survived the later restoration. A P. Mobil concert on 23 September 1984 is described as the end of the Youth Park. The building was closed that year and decayed, and it was listed among the hundred most endangered monuments in the world.

A government decree of 2011 launched its reconstruction. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the first phase reopened on 3 April 2014, and the second, with an event centre, underground garage and Renaissance garden, followed on 29 August 2014. Excavations during the work found medieval and Ottoman-era objects, remains of cannon foundries that operated here from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, and, according to the building's own history page, several hundred carved stone and cast-iron bullets, probably from the 1686 recapture of Buda. Restorers also found an old lock with its broken key still inside, which has since been shown in several exhibitions.

The gardens are the part most visitors walk through. The Visit Buda Castle page mentions a Triton Fountain, a rose garden and stretches of old castle walls, and describes the building by the Danube bank as a home for exhibitions and cultural events. Do not confuse the bazaar with the Várkert-kiosk, a separate Ybl building nearby; the Buda Castle history notes that only these two of his works there survive.
Good to know
The gardens lie at the foot of Castle Hill beside the Danube bank, so they combine easily with a visit to the Castle District above.
Check the official Várkert Bazár site for current exhibitions, events and visiting conditions, as the building hosts cultural programmes.

When the building reopened in 2014, the Budapest History Museum's exhibition Ostromok és hétköznapok showed archaeological finds from the excavations in the southern palaces; check the official site for what is currently on show.

historyIntro: The Várkert Bazár was planned in the early 1870s and built between 1875 and 1883 to designs by Miklós Ybl. It then passed through studios, schools and a rock-concert venue, was closed in 1984, and was restored in 2014.

historySections.heading: Ybl's complex below the palace, 1875 to 1883

children.text: The building's own history page says the idea of a representative building complex and ornamental garden at the foot of Castle Hill arose in the early 1870s, and that Miklós Ybl was given the task of drawing the final plans. The neo-Renaissance complex was built between 1875 and 1883. A history of Buda Castle describes an open arcade with pavilions, stairways, ramps and two blocks of flats. The arcades were meant for shops and workshops, and the gardens were laid out to keep an open view of the Danube from the Royal Palace. Ybl died in 1891, before the palace reconstruction he had planned was finished.

historySections.heading: Studios, schools and a Youth Park, 1884 to 1984

children.text: According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the north wing housed a craftswomen's training workshop from 1883 to 1888, the Historical Portrait Gallery from 1890 to 1895 and a women's painting school from about 1890 until 1918. From 1884 the sculptor Alajos Stróbl had a studio in the arcade, the first of about eighty artists who worked there over the next century. The building was heavily damaged in the Second World War. From 1961 it became the Budai Ifjúsági Park, a venue for pop and rock concerts. A staircase wall collapsed during an Edda concert in 1980, and the Youth Park ended in 1984, when the building was closed.

After 1984 the building decayed, and a Visit Hungary article says it was listed among the hundred most endangered monuments in the world. Several plans for its reconstruction and reuse were drawn up before Government Decree 1375 of 2011 launched the reconstruction, with work beginning in summer 2013. Excavations found medieval and Ottoman-era objects, remains of cannon foundries of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries and, according to the building's own history page, several hundred carved stone and cast-iron bullets, probably from the 1686 recapture of Buda. The Triton fountain was restored. The first phase reopened on 3 April 2014, and a second phase, with an event centre, an underground garage and a Renaissance garden, followed on 29 August 2014.

stories.title: Franz Joseph and the view he rarely saw

children.text: Visit Hungary records a story told about the gardens: according to legend, Emperor Franz Joseph rarely enjoyed the Danube view that the Neo-Renaissance gardens were designed to keep open, because he never stayed overnight in the Castle. The article presents this as a legend, not as a documented fact.

name: Clark Ádám Square and the 0 km Stone
description: The roundabout at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, named after the engineer Adam Clark and home to the limestone 0 km stone from which Hungary's main roads are numbered. The Buda Castle Funicular and the tunnel under Castle Hill start here.

children.text: Clark Ádám tér is the square at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, below Castle Hill. Visit Buda Castle calls it a symbolic starting point: the limestone 0 km stone stands here, beside the lower station of the Buda Castle Funicular, and the kilometre numbering of several of Hungary's main roads is counted from it. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it marks the start of the first-class main roads except routes 1 and 8, and that the square lies at the entrance of the Buda tunnel.

The square has had several names. In the 1860s it was also called Népszínház tér, after the Buda People's Theatre that stood there, and from the mid-1870s Lánchíd tér, Chain Bridge Square. In 1912 it was renamed after Adam Clark, the Scottish engineer who designed the Chain Bridge and the tunnel. Hungarian Wikipedia calls it Budapest's first uniform neo-Renaissance square.

War and rebuilding changed it. The Budai Takarékpénztár building, designed by Miklós Ybl, was hit by a bomb in the Second World War. Hungarian Wikipedia says it was demolished in 1949 while the roundabout was being built, whereas We Love Budapest says the damaged parts came down in 1948 and a remaining torso only in 1990; a hotel now stands on the site. The Lánchíd Palota is the only original building left standing on the square. The square and the area around the 0 km stone were renovated in July 2014.

The stone itself is a limestone sculpture about three metres tall, with a zero sign and the letters KM on its pedestal. English Wikipedia credits the present sculpture to Miklós Borsos and dates it to 1975. It was not the first monument on the spot: in 1932 a statue of the Virgin Mary by Körmendi, put up by the Hungária Automobil Club, was the first monument here. Sources differ on its fate: English Wikipedia says the Second World War destroyed it, while We Love Budapest says it survived the siege but was removed by the communist authorities. From 1953 until the present sculpture replaced it, a sculpture of a worker stood here.
Good to know
The square is the lower terminus of the Buda Castle Funicular; check the official funicular page for its current operating status and tickets.
From the stone you can walk onto the Chain Bridge or into the Castle Hill area; the Buda tunnel entrance is at the square.
The roundabout is busy with traffic, so use the marked crossings when approaching the stone and take photographs from the small park around it.

historyIntro: The Zero Kilometre Stone at Clark Ádám Square is the point from which distances in Hungary are measured, and the spot has held several monuments in its time.

children.text: The present sculpture was erected in 1975 and is the work of Miklós Borsos. It is a three-metre limestone monument that represents Kilometre Zero in Hungary, and its pedestal carries the inscription 'KM' for kilometres. It stands in a small park at Clark Ádám Square, at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, below Buda Castle.

historySections.heading: A spot with a changing monument

children.text: The country's road zero point is said to have first been marked at the threshold of the Buda Royal Palace. HVG says the milestone was later moved near the newly opened Chain Bridge, and English Wikipedia dates this to 1849, although the source it cites does not mention the move. A Madonna statue by Eugene Kormendi was set up on the spot in 1932; English Wikipedia says it was destroyed in the Second World War, but other sources say it survived the siege and was removed later. A sculpture of a worker stood there from 1953 until the present monument replaced it.

name: Hungarian Heritage House
description: A national institute for Hungarian folk culture based in the former Budai Vigadó on Corvin Square, built in 1898-1900. It runs folk dance houses, craft courses, concerts, exhibitions and archival work, and it is also the base of the Hungarian State Folk Ensemble.

children.text: The Hungarian Heritage House, in Hungarian the Hagyományok Háza, is an institute of national significance that works to preserve the folk traditions of the Carpathian Basin. It was established in 2001. Its mission includes bringing back small cultural elements that have faded or are fading and keeping them alive in today's cultural life. Its activities include stage folk dance, handicraft classes, folk craft arts, archiving of folklore footage, live storytelling and folk arts education for young people.

Its home is the former Budai Vigadó, an entertainment hall in Buda at Corvin tér 8, standing on Fő utca between Batthyány tér and Clark Ádám tér. The institute's own page says it was built between 1898 and 1900 by Aladár Árkay and Mór Kallina and was designed as a cultural complex for Buda's middle class, with a theatre, library, cafe and restaurant. It has an eclectic exterior with a relatively simple facade and rich Art Nouveau ornamentation inside, including a columned hall with a wide marble staircase and an ornamented lounge.

The house runs a permanent dance house series in its glass-roofed atrium. The institute says the first Budapest dance house was held in May 1972, based on the experience of the dance houses of Szék, a village in Transylvania. Its own dance houses focus on teaching, with courses on a region's dances followed by a ball with regional musicians. The Hungarian State Folk Ensemble, which marked its 70th anniversary around the time of the institute's 20th, is part of the house.

Other activities include folk craft training, folk music and dance camps and a museum, according to the institute's own website. The Buda Castle District attractions listing describes it as a place where folk tradition appears in a living, present-day form, with dance performances, concerts, exhibitions, craft programmes and community events.
Good to know
Check the Heritage House website for the current dance house series, exhibitions, concerts and tickets, since programmes run by season.
The institute's page suggests metro line 2 to Batthyány tér followed by a short walk south on Fő utca, or bus 86 to Szilágyi Dezső tér, or tram 19 or 41 to Halász utca.
The Hungarian Heritage House is a different institution from museums nearby, so look for the Corvin tér 8 address when you navigate.

historyIntro: The Hungarian Heritage House was established in 2001 in the Budai Vigadó, a Buda entertainment hall built in 1898-1900. It draws on the dance house movement that began in Budapest in 1972 and on the Hungarian State Folk Ensemble founded in the early 1950s.

children.text: The Heritage House's own page says its building was the historic Vigadó, an entertainment hall, of Buda. It was built between 1898 and 1900 by Aladár Árkay and Mór Kallina as a cultural complex for Buda's middle class, with a theatre, library, cafe and restaurant. The exterior is eclectic with a relatively simple facade, while the interior has rich Art Nouveau ornamentation, including a columned hall with a wide marble staircase. The page does not describe the building's later history or restoration, so those details should be checked separately.

historySections.heading: Dance houses and a state folk ensemble

children.text: The Heritage House's page on its dance house says the first Budapest dance house was held in May 1972, based on the experience of the dance houses of Szék in Transylvania. UNESCO's own page says the táncház method was selected in 2011 for its Register of Good Safeguarding Practices, as a Hungarian model for transmitting intangible heritage. The Hungarian State Folk Ensemble is described as the first professional folk dance ensemble in Hungary. Miklós Rábai was chosen in 1950 to establish its dance chorus, and its inaugural performance, with the Moiseyev Ensemble, took place on 4 April 1951 at the Opera House.

The Hungarian Heritage House was established in 2001 as an institute of national significance based in the Budai Vigadó on Corvin Square. Its mission is to preserve folk traditions of the Carpathian Basin and bring back small cultural elements that have faded or are fading. A February 2021 report said the institute marked 20 years in 2021, a double jubilee with the 70th anniversary of the Folk Ensemble, which also works from the building. Its activities include stage folk dance, handicraft classes, archiving of folklore footage and folk arts education.
